en: Compiled by Shi Dunlun, *Lunben* (Excerpts from Treatises), Volume Eighty.
The preceding section concludes the explanation of the first five of the sixteen chapters of the *Ratnakūṭa Sūtra*. From here below, the [sixth]...
Sixth, regarding the establishment of the trainings within correct practice,
there are two parts. First,
a general question-and-answer section that enumerates the thirteen middle-way practices.
Regarding the subsequent inquiry into the specific interpretation:

among those previously mentioned, the bodhisattva is one who has first taken as a basis the sūtras of the Śrāvaka vehicle that teach conventional reality and provisional meaning, and who has thoroughly mastered them.
Relying solely on the emptiness of persons while not yet seeing the emptiness of phenomena,
they know it is not ultimate,
and thus they transcend that state.

Furthermore, diligently studying the definitive sutras that accord with the two emptinesses and the principles of the two truths within the Mahāyāna is called the practice of the Middle Way. Why is this so?
Thus, the reason why the sūtras of the Hīnayāna are of provisional meaning (*neyārtha*) while the sūtras of the Mahāyāna are of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) has been stated as the question;
what follows below clarifies the intended answer.
Because it penetrates the practice of the thirteenfold Middle Way within the Mahāyāna, it is of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).
This refers to the enumeration of the thirteen names.
Regarding their individual explanations:
First, regarding the explanation of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*): Master Jingbei said,
"The statement 'because it cannot be apprehended through any single characteristic' means..."
The falsely imagined real self cannot be found. Below,
it is clarified that when one seeks within the three factors— the internal sense faculties, the external objects, and the intermediate six consciousnesses—
no real self exists at all.
That which cannot be apprehended as a sentient being refers to the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*).
As for "distinct phenomena," it refers to...
This refers to the distinct phenomena of the six external sense objects.
As for the act of experiencing them,
it is the six consciousnesses experiencing pleasure and pain amidst the sense faculties and their objects.
Master Tai said:
"This refers to the principle that the substance of a real self is non-existent, yet there is the personhood of a bodhisattva;
it concerns the single matter of a sentient being."
Among the three types of sentient beings, there are the phenomena of the distinctions between the aggregates (skandhas), elements (dhātus), and bases (āyatanas);
and the phenomena of the six sense organs, the six consciousnesses, and the enjoyment of the six objects.

Whether it be the six internal sense organs or the six external objects, apart from these three categories, no real self can be found at all within the midst of ordinary beings' arbitrary conceptualizations.
Second interpretation:

Regarding the statement that "the person-selflessness (pudgala-nairātmya) is apprehended by way of a single characteristic," it means that the principle of suchness (tathatā) revealed by person-selflessness exists.
Therefore, it is said that "it can be attained.

This means that while foolish people universally conceptualize a permanent, real self within the three factors of sense organ, object, and consciousness—claiming such a self cannot be found—one can indeed attain the principle of its distinct nature and characteristics.
The principle that the nature of true suchness (tathatā) is distinct from the false self can be established.
Question:
What is the difference between emptiness (śūnyatā) and selflessness (anātman)?
The commentary explains:
The absence of a self within the aggregates is called "emptiness" (śūnyatā);
the fact that the substance of the aggregates is not the self is called "selflessness" (anātman).
Regarding the third, the emptiness of the dharma of liberation,
Bei Jing says: "That is,
within the dharmas of the dependent and the perfected..."
Because that imputed nature of phenomena— such as permanence, impermanence, and so forth— which follows linguistic expression does not exist,
it is called "emptiness of phenomena" (*dharma-śūnyatā*). Tái says:
The nature of arising and ceasing, which is impermanent, regarding that which is grasped through pervasive conceptualization is not included within the five categories; therefore,
it is not apprehended at all.
This is intended to clarify that the nature of the dharmas and self as conceived by the parikalpita (imagined) nature is empty and non-existent, such that they cannot be apprehended at all;
however, it does not clarify that the true suchness of the absence of dharmas and self is actually existent and yet unapprehendable.
Fourth is the understanding of the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*).
This refers to that which is manifested by the selflessness of phenomena, from the single characteristic up to the sphere of activity of noble wisdom (*āryajñāna*).
It is the suchness (*tathatā*) manifested by the selflessness of phenomena, which is the sphere of activity of noble wisdom.
Therefore, it is possible to inquire about the Dharma. Question:
What is the difference between emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*)?
The commentary explains:

Based on the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) and the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), the absence of those falsely imagined determinate dharmas is called the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*).
That these two natures are not objects of sentient beings' grasping is called the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*).
Furthermore,
it is explained that phenomena arising from dependent causes and conditions are like magical illusions, lacking any determinate nature.
It is called the emptiness of phenomena (dharmasūnyatā).
The perfected nature (pariniṣpannasvabhāva), which is wondrously free from existence and non-existence,
is called the emptiness of phenomena.
These two natures do not possess an intrinsic substance or function by way of being grasped; this is called the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*).
Therefore, the *Saṃgrahaṇī* states: "If one clings to all phenomena as having substance and function, this is called the self of phenomena (*dharmātman*)."
To clarify that phenomena lack an intrinsic nature or essence is called the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*).
Below, it is clarified that because of the six characteristics, the ineffable internal realization of suchness, which is manifested by the absence of "mine," is revealed.
It differs from the nature of ordinary people who follow verbal designations;
therefore, it can be apprehended.
The six characteristics are as stated in the text.
Regarding the five types of increase in understanding,
Jing says:
"There are eight distinctions."
First, the adherence to permanence;
second, the adherence to having a fixed nature, which is also an exaggeration (samāropa) even if it concerns impermanence;
third, the adherence to permanence and the adherence to a self due to [misconstruing] causes, which are exaggerations.
1) Due to the adherence to the four causes, one clings to impermanence;
2) due to the adherence to existence, one clings to non-self; 3) due to the adherence to non-self, one superimposes a real mind;
4) due to the adherence to a self, one superimposes an unreal mind.
The section beginning with "This further has two kinds" below is a re-explanation of the fifth and sixth [points].
First, regarding "certainty":
First, fixed adherence to an object.
Second, seeking: this refers to the mind that seeks out and moves toward objects, whether real or unreal.
Within this, first, that upon which the universal imagination (*parikalpa*) relies is sought;
and that which corresponds to the universal imagination clarifies the seeker.
Below this, it is explained in detail.
First, it is explained that when one seeks with a mind that does not grasp at reality,
there are five faults in the afflicted phenomena that are to be remedied;
namely, those that involve inversion.
To conceive of a self where there is no self is what is meant by "vain proliferation" (prapañca);
it refers to wandering delusively outside of reality.
Regarding those who initiate unwholesome conduct:
it is because of this that karma is produced;
as for "coarseness" (dauṣṭhulya), it refers to this.
Arising from afflictions and karma,
the coarse and heavy [elements] increase;
such is the nature of impermanence.
Delusion and karma give rise to birth, increasing impermanence and suffering.

Below, it is clarified that the grasping at a real mind and the attachment to a real path capable of removing [defilements] and achieving purity also constitute the parikalpita-svabhāva (imagined nature).
Therefore, it is said that within those pure dharmas which serve as antidotes, there is a seventh [type of grasping]:
grasping at the mind as truly existent and superimposing it as a basis, and further grasping at goodness and so forth, up to grasping at purity and superimposing it.

Eighth, there is the adherence to the superimposition of an unreal mind as a basis, and further, the adherence to the superimposition of unwholesome states and so forth, up to the adherence to the superimposition of defilements.
Regarding these superimpositions, the bodhisattva does not cling at all.
The distinctions have already been explained.
Next, the augmentation of intrinsic nature is clarified;
this refers to the grasping at the substantial essence of all phenomena as being existent.
Tài says:
"The principle of person-non-self realized by the two vehicles is merely the characteristic of True Suchness (tathatā-lakṣaṇa), not the actual True Suchness."

Within the context of the five matters, the principle of personal selflessness (*pudgala-nairātmya*) realized by those prior to the stages and by the two vehicles among the three natures is subsumed under the matter of "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*).
If one clings to this as being *tathatā* (suchness), [it is a misconception].
This is also the extreme of superimposition.
Therefore, that fourth superimposition takes as its basis the fifth [extreme],
which is the superimposition of the principle of the two kinds of selflessness.
They grasp the untainted contemplative mind that realizes the two kinds of selflessness as being truly real.
However, this untainted contemplative mind is a provisional existence arising from causes and conditions;
yet they cling to it as having a real, fixed nature.
Therefore, it is called "superimposition" (*samāropa*).
This refers specifically to the fourth [type of] superimposition regarding objects and the fifth [type of] superimposition regarding the mind.
The sixth [extreme] is the view of a self with a fixed nature,
which takes as its basis the superimposition of two selves; because it is an unreal mental state,
it is called the extreme of superimposition (*samāropa-anta*).
Thus, one knows that the mind which clings to a self is a false attachment and is therefore unreal.
Nevertheless, there is the false attachment to an intrinsic nature, which is called "superimposition" (*samāropa*).
This clinging is of two kinds.
First, the mind that resolutely clings to what is unreal;
second, the seeking through skillful means.
As for "seeking":
Regarding the basis of determination— namely, improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanasikāra*) and the associated attention (*manasikāra*) that accords with it—
the following explains the principles of investigation.
One investigates five faults within the unreal mental afflictions (*saṃkleśa-dharma*) that constitute the objects of counteraction.
Because there exists a self-nature that can be remedied,
there exists a purifying dharma capable of acting as an antidote.
This citation of the antidote serves to demonstrate that the obstacle possesses a self-nature.
This is also a superimposition by an unreal mind.

Regarding the seventh [cause]: because the preceding fifth [cause] takes the mind that perceives the reality of untainted contemplation as its basis, the seventh [cause] arises, which clings to the existence of a substantial nature in all untainted wholesome dharmas produced by that real, untainted mind.
This extends even to the grasping at pure nirvāṇa as having an intrinsic nature.
Because the eighth [grasping] relies upon the sixth grasping—the view of a self that possesses a fixed nature—it gives rise to the eighth grasping:
the notion that the various unwholesome dharmas produced by the view of a self possess an intrinsic nature.
...up to the point that one grasps at the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the defiled phenomena of birth and death (*saṃsāra-saṃkleśa-dharma*) as being moistened by the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*).
Question:
In the preceding explanation of the selflessness of persons (*pudgala-nairātmya*), it was shown that a single characteristic (*eka-lakṣaṇa*) is perceivable. What is this?
Why is the fifth position, which maintains that there is no self, considered an extreme of superimposition?
The answer is:
the former [position] was based on the fact that suchness, as revealed by the absence of self, is truly existent.
Therefore, it is said that [the self] can be apprehended.
If the meaning of "no-self" were merely the non-existence of a phenomenon, then,
as determined in the second fascicle of the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī*, one would have to explain how the view of a self takes a non-arising mind as its object.
If one clings to non-existence as being existent, it constitutes the superimposition (samāropa).
Da says: "That which is the basis for pervasive conceptualization (parikalpita)..."
The faculties that serve as the basis for conceptualization,
as well as those associated with pervasive conceptualization,
refer to the mental factors (caitta) associated with the mind that performs conceptualization.
"Grasping at the wholesome, etc.
includes the unobscured-unarisen; "grasping at the unwholesome, etc.
includes the obscured-unarisen.
Sixth, the statement regarding the diminution of conviction:

"That is, one gives rise to conviction regarding the selflessness of those false dharmas," refers to hearing the teaching that the nature of the parikalpita-svabhāva (imagined nature) is fundamentally non-existent.
Consequently, one would hold that both the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) and the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) are entirely non-existent.
This is a perverted grasping of emptiness (*durgṛhīta-śūnyatā*),
termed the "false selflessness of phenomena" (*mithyā-dharmanairātmya*).
Regarding the seventh, the clear realization of the analytical dharma (*dharmavibhāga-abhisamaya*),
Jing says:
"By means of three aspects."
First, the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is unapprehendable.
To speak [of it] in relation to those things is the foremost instance of superimposition.
Regarding the fourth point concerning the nature of arising:
among the aforementioned four types of superimposition (*samāropa*), this refers to the superimposition of the non-existence of a self.
Second, their distinct characteristics cannot be apprehended.
Third, because of that habitual cultivation, one penetrates reality as it is.
To say that "self-nature is unattainable herein" means that self-nature cannot be found to possess the two divisions of arising and ceasing.
Because one has become habituated to the non-apprehension of these two,
one spontaneously penetrates the suchness (tathatā) manifested by signlessness.

This means that through the wisdom personally realized within oneself, one penetrates it by not attending to, not conceptualizing, and not analytically investigating the characteristics of its own nature, but rather through the application of spontaneous practice.
T'ai says:

"Thus, within that established conceptualization of phenomena and the fourth stage of the eighth clear realization (*abhisamaya*), the self-nature of the matter of the birth-body (*janma-śarīra*) cannot be apprehended; this constitutes the first characteristic."
In the section on the dedication of the lower clear realizations,
four types of remedies are distinguished.
First, the remedy that is capable of counteracting.
Second, it is the antidote to that which is to be remedied;
third, it is the antidote to karma leading to further existence;
and fourth, it is the antidote to the body of birth.
Regarding the dedication of the eight liberations into the nature of great bodhi,
Jing says: First,
he generally clarifies the dharma-realization (*dharmābhisamaya*) as that which can treat both the remedial and the remediated.
This means that because the antidote obtained through the discernment of a single aspect does not sever that which is to be countered,
the antidotes and the counteracted are now explained individually below.
There are three successive expositions.
The first states that among these, the "remedy" and the "object to be remedied" refer to emptiness as the antidote to afflictions;
if one is to sever afflictions, it is only by entering through the gate of liberation of emptiness and realizing *tathatā* (suchness) that one can truly eliminate delusions.
The wishless (*apraṇihita*) is the remedy for having wishes.
The wishless is the antidote to the longing for birth and death (*saṃsāra*).
The signless gate of liberation (*animitta-vimokṣamukha*) is the antidote to the ten signs (*daśa-nimitta*).
All such things are called "without an agent.
The three gates of liberation counteract birth and death;
within the realm of birth and death, they are termed "without an agent."
Secondly, furthermore,
that which serves as the antidote to future karma is emptiness.
Furthermore, that which is the flow of the physical body is wishlessness (*apraṇihita*).
It is the antidote to the flow of momentary birth and death (*kṣaṇika-saṃsāra-pravṛtti*), and so forth.
This is signlessness (*animitta*).
From here below is the third section:
because the preceding emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and so forth reveal cessation (*nirodha*) and nirvāṇa, which serve as the antidote by overturning the aforementioned saṃsāra.
To say that the practice of cessation-nirvāṇa lacks intrinsic nature,
and further that it takes the cyclic flow of birth and death as its counteragent,
is out of compassion for sentient beings.
Therefore, one intentionally retains afflictions to undergo birth and transform beings;
by practicing so as to increase merit, one proceeds toward Great Bodhi.
Beiyun said:
The preceding liberation door of emptiness does not merely sever afflictions;
it can also sever karma and its maturation.
The treatise states:
"From this point onward, the meaning of the subsequent passages is as follows:
the arising of all bodies is collectively termed the 'flowing and turning of the birth-body' (*jāti-kāya-saṃsāra*)."
Because they arise moment by moment,
they are said to flow and revolve from instant to instant;
this summarizes the three gates of liberation.
Therefore, it is called "nirvāṇa-practice" because it lacks intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Thus, the cyclic flow of birth and death (*saṃsāra*) is that which is to be remedied.
Ninth interpretation.
For a practitioner who acts in this way, the afflictions and various sufferings do not entangle the mind; it is difficult for them not to permanently sever that which is to be remedied.
By means of the contemplation of the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*), they perceive its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*);
thus, they are unstained and free from suffering.
The distinction between the ten types of understanding and the two types of resolve regarding selflessness is as follows;
it is by way of four aspects.
First, the distinction of vision.
This refers to those who, abiding in the realization of the selflessness of persons and in nirvana, give rise to the overweening pride of annihilation regarding their future bodies.
Such individuals, prior to the path of seeing, have practiced the contemplation of the selflessness of persons.
Based on this, the wisdom of contemplation gives rise to conceit, namely the thought:
"I have attained nirvāṇa; henceforth my body shall not arise.
Furthermore, regarding the objects of apprehension, up to the point of "not having correctly examined the objects of knowledge," [this refers to the aforementioned state].
Ordinary beings cling to objects, perceiving both the self and the mind that conceives as truly existent.
Those of the Two Vehicles merely falsely impute a divine self to the grasped object and observe it to be non-existent.
Not observing that the mind which performs the calculation is itself empty by nature in accordance with verbal expression,
it is therefore called "not skillfully observing the object of knowledge.
Because of this clinging to all phenomena, one seeks the cessation of afflictions.
To cling to the existence of all phenomena while seeking to sever afflictions, yet failing to realize the emptiness of phenomena,
is called "differentiation through views.
The Bodhisattvas, however, do not act in this way.

The second is the distinction of extreme remoteness and diminution, which refers to the loss and destruction of the abiding in the selflessness of the person (*pudgala-nairātmya*) and even the two types of grasping regarding the past and future, and so forth.
Jingyun said:
There is a certain class of people who, upon hearing it said that the self of parikalpita (imagined nature) is empty,
then cling to the view that the aggregates which serve as the objective referent of the view of self are also empty.
Regarding the view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*), it is classified as "inferior" (*hīna*);

regarding the view of inferiority (*ūnadṛṣṭi*), it is classified as "inferior-inferior" (*hīna-hīna*). Regarding the view of emptiness (*śūnyatādṛṣṭi*), it is classified as "inferior-middle-inferior" (*hīna-madhya-hīna*).
The meaning of the following passage is explained by two causes and conditions:
first, one is not liberated from suffering because,
being attached to the view of emptiness, one does not cultivate the causes for the cessation of suffering.
Regarding the second point, concerning the loss of the two types of attachment— prior and posterior— to abiding in suffering:
the prior [attachment] relies on the teaching to give rise to the view of non-self,
which, like the view of self, clings to the idea that dependent origination does not exist.
This is called the loss and destruction resulting from two kinds of attachment regarding the past and the future.
Third, regarding the distinction of losing one's way in cessation:
this refers to those who abide in the selflessness of persons and even pursue total annihilation.
Those of the two vehicles who have already realized the selflessness of persons,
upon hearing that the self-nature of all phenomena is empty according to how they are expressed by words, give rise to fear and alarm, thinking that nirvana is the annihilation of phenomena.
They are unable to understand that while the imagined nature— which consists of phenomena as expressed by words— is ultimately empty, the other two natures remain.

Fourth is the differentiation of delusion regarding the mind; that is to say, such delusion regarding abandonment, up to being inverted by things such as the inversion of perception (*saṃjñā-viparyāsa*).
Although one does not grasp at a person (*pudgala*), [one is still deluded].
Nevertheless, they remain inverted by the three inversions of dharma-attachment, conceptualization, and views.
Regarding the eleventh [point], the nature of the cause of liberation, it says:
"In this context, the observation of the grasper extends to the momentary."
That is to say, one observes that phenomena arising dependently through other-causes and conditions undergo momentary arising and ceasing,
and are devoid of the verbally-constructed nature of pervasive conceptualization.
Regarding the phrase "one who penetrates this as it truly is until certain knowledge arises":
because one penetrates that the imagined nature and the grasped and grasper are unattainable,
internally realized perfected nature (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva) arises as certain knowledge.
The twelfth is the emptiness of reaching the limit (*prāntakoṭika-śūnyatā*).
Regarding the statement that "that which appears here as it truly is exists until the momentary," this means that by means of the wisdom of selflessness (*anātma-jñāna*),
one does not apprehend the capacity of the thoroughly imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).
At a later time, when conditions for karma and afflictions arise, they follow the mental aspects that resemble karma and afflictions;
these are known in accordance with their objects without further conceptual construction.
One does not cling to either those mental aspects or the ineffable intrinsic nature of the original objects—the karma and afflictions themselves.
Thus, both the image and its underlying essence are phenomena that arise and perish moment by moment;
they differ from the parikalpita (imagined nature), which is non-momentary and devoid of arising or ceasing.
Thirteenth is the majestic power of understanding emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
Regarding the statement, "In this context, 'abandonment' extends to all karma and afflictions," it is as that sūtra says:
"It is like a dark room of a thousand years."
Just as a single moment of light from a lamp or candle can entirely dispel darkness,
so too, if the light of wisdom arises, it can dispel the afflictions and karmic obscurations that have existed since beginningless time.
A single thought-moment severs it.
This concludes the seventh great section:
explaining the distinctions between the superior trainings of the śrāvakas and bodhisattvas.
First, a brief enumeration:
there are four types of śrāvakas, and the distinctions in the training of these śrāvakas and bodhisattvas consist of thirteen types.
Second, the formal explanation.
First, the four types of śrāvakas are explained;
next, their distinctions are explained.
Within the explanation of the four types of śrāvakas:
First, the four names are listed;
second, the names are cited and explained.
From "Those śrāvakas of overweening pride" up to "who reckon [themselves] as pure."
If one relies on the Hinayana teachings,
the śrāvaka is the ultimate;
now, relying on the Mahayana teachings...
The Śrāvaka is likewise not ultimate;

having attained fulfillment in the knowledge of the selflessness of persons (pudgala-nairātmya) within the stage of the Śrāvaka vehicle, they have yet to accomplish the study of the selflessness of phenomena (dharma-nairātmya).
Therefore, this is termed "clinging to the false view regarding the knowledge of the selflessness of phenomena."
However, to actually be unpurified yet to reckon oneself as purified is the overweening pride of claiming to have attained what one has not attained.
As for the phrase "like the two princes": [it refers to this].
These are the śrāvakas and bodhisattvas.
Regarding "being born in a similar state," it means that they equally sever the afflictions and realize liberation.
That which experiences royal happiness is nirvāṇa. First,
regarding those who are thoroughly skilled in the administration of statecraft, the arts, and so forth—
The Buddha is named the Dharma King.
The teachings of the Tripiṭaka are called the administration and deliberation;
the activities for the benefit of others are called the arts and crafts.
The Bodhisattva well understands this;
the Śrāvaka does not. This is so within the context of the distinctions in their respective understandings.
First, the distinctions are enumerated, totaling thirteen;
next, they are explained individually.
Although thirteen are listed, [the following applies].
In the commentary, twelve points are explained by combining the two gates of "lineage" (*gotra*) and "maintaining the seed.
Therefore, it says: "Furthermore, those śrāvakas are indeed sons of the Buddha.
Although śrāvakas cultivate their realization by taking *nirvāṇa* as their object of focus, they are not [true] sons of the Buddha.
Although a bodhisattva focuses their attention on inferior objects such as the cycle of birth and death and sentient beings, they are nonetheless a child of the Buddha;
furthermore, even though a śrāvaka may apply themselves with diligent effort, they remain contrary to that [bodhisattva path].
Although a śrāvaka may apply himself with diligent effort and attain stability of mind through contemplation of the Four Noble Truths,
he does not achieve the characteristics of the Buddha-lineage.
Therefore, they are called those without the spiritual lineage (*agotra*).
Because the Buddhas do not long-term embrace them,
they are called those who do not uphold the lineage.

Furthermore, regarding the statement that "the Śrāvakas reach that [state] because it is accomplished through this," the meaning is the same as the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*’s description of the "first dharma" (*agra-dharma*) as being preeminent.
At all times, the Tathāgata is superior to the Śrāvakas.
The Bodhisattva’s aspiration for the Buddha is even more superior than the Buddha himself;
for that Buddha is brought to fulfillment through the accumulation [of merit] by this Bodhisattva.
It is just as the "Supreme Mundane Dharma" (laukikāgradharma) is preeminent because it opens the way for the arising of the Noble Path.
Furthermore, regarding the statement "by two conditions... even unto enabling liberation," this explains why the Bodhisattva is superior to the Buddha.
First, because by means of the causal conditions of practicing the six perfections, this Bodhisattva brings forth the fruit of enlightenment.
Second, because once enlightenment is attained, one brings sentient beings to maturity;
alternatively, one may bring sentient beings to maturity and mature the Buddha-dharma simultaneously.
It is by virtue of these two conditions.
Therefore, by attracting awakening and maturing sentient beings,
he is superior even to the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, it is explained thus:
The former [section] distinguishes superiority in relation to the fruit of Buddhahood; this [section] distinguishes superiority in relation to the Śrāvakas.
Those Bodhisattvas are superior to the Śrāvakas for two reasons.
"For example, there is a person who has already...
and so forth; this is the analogy. "One who is capable of discernment" refers to the subject of the illustration.
Cultivating the causes is likened to [the process],
and being able to ripen them is likened to attaining the fruit.
Being skillful in cultivation,
it is called the marvelous awakening-wisdom;
having fulfilled one's own practice, one is able to benefit all sentient beings.
This is not like the śrāvakas, who, after attaining the fruit, remain in silent enjoyment;
therefore it is said, "He sits upright while eating.
This concludes the eighth section of the Great Gate.
This explains how the Bodhisattva, having skillfully studied mundane and supramundane knowledge, benefits others.
Within this, there is first a general summary and subsequently a detailed analysis.
Within the section on distinctions:
first, mundane wisdom is elucidated;
subsequently, supramundane wisdom is elucidated.
Regarding the preceding section:
mundane wisdom that brings to rest and subdues superior and middling levels of affliction pertains to the stage prior to the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
Regarding those who have gone forth and who, with respect to that which is not liberation, cling to it as liberation and rely upon it as their nature,
there are four points.
The first is the nature of reliance on wrong views.
Second, the state of non-attention toward the basis of meditative training (*samādhi-śikṣā*) due to those two and their underlying wrong views;
third, the state of being a basis for the aspiration for future existence (*punarbhava*);
